reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: Female sexual dysfunction spans disorders of desire, arousal, orgasm, and sexual pain, and is only a clinical diagnosis when the problem is persistent and causes personal distress
The female sexual response is better understood as a circular, intimacy-driven model rather than a rigid linear sequence, so context and relationship factors are central
Causes are typically multifactorial, combining biological, psychological, and interpersonal contributors that should all be explored
Hormonal changes, especially the oestrogen decline of menopause, commonly reduce arousal and lubrication and contribute to genitourinary and pain symptoms
Many common medications, particularly serotonergic antidepressants, and chronic illnesses such as diabetes, depression, and vascular disease impair sexual function
A sensitive, open history that legitimises the concern is essential, as patients often will not raise the topic themselves

Management addresses reversible contributors, optimises relationship and psychological factors, and considers psychosexual therapy alongside targeted treatments such as local oestrogen for genitourinary symptoms
Persistent pain with intercourse points towards specific disorders such as vaginismus or dyspareunia that require directed assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Female sexual function integrates neurological, vascular, hormonal, and psychological systems. Sexual arousal depends on genital vasocongestion and lubrication mediated by autonomic and nitric-oxide pathways, while desire and orgasm involve central dopaminergic, serotonergic, and hormonal modulation. Dysfunction arises when any of these are disrupted: oestrogen deficiency thins and dries the vaginal epithelium and reduces blood flow, vascular and neurological disease (as in diabetes) impairs the genital response, and medications such as SSRIs blunt desire and orgasm. Psychological factors including depression, anxiety, past trauma, body image, and relationship conflict powerfully influence desire and arousal, and pain disorders can create a self-reinforcing cycle of anticipatory anxiety and avoidance. The circular, context-dependent nature of female sexual response means these factors interact rather than act in isolation.
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive biopsychosocial and sexual history including relationship context
Review of medications, particularly antidepressants, and chronic medical conditions
Pelvic examination to identify atrophy, pain, or structural causes
Targeted endocrine assessment where indicated, including menopausal status
Screening for depression, anxiety, and history of sexual trauma
redFlags: Sexual pain or bleeding suggesting an underlying gynaecological pathology
History of sexual abuse or trauma requiring sensitive, specialised support
New sexual dysfunction accompanying signs of significant systemic or neurological disease
reference.prognosis: Outcomes are generally good when contributing factors are identified and addressed; genitourinary symptoms of menopause respond well to local oestrogen, medication-related effects may improve with adjustment, and psychosexual and relationship interventions can substantially help desire and arousal disorders.
pitfalls: Not asking about sexual health, so distressing problems go unrecognised
Attributing dysfunction to a single cause when it is usually multifactorial
Overlooking medication, especially antidepressants, as a reversible contributor
Neglecting relationship and psychological dimensions in favour of a purely biomedical approach
